note.note:
History:
- Chief complaint: Several days of severe diarrhoea with fever and vomiting; abdominal pain around the umbilicus.
- Onset and duration: Symptoms began about 3 days ago and have persisted.
- Course: Stool currently very loose/watery progressing to frequent episodes (today at least 4 bowel movements). Fever felt hot to touch. Multiple vomiting episodes with inability to keep any fluids down (including water, tea).
- Associated symptoms: Nausea/vomiting; abdominal cramping centered around the periumbilical area; pain worsens with urge to stool.
- Hydration and intake: Attempted oral rehydration salts (ORS) 3 times daily for ~2 days; unable to retain fluids due to vomiting; last urine was produced about 1 hour ago.
- Exposures and context: Brother with similar symptoms; possible school outbreak; no travel abroad; living with mother and brother.
- Medical and surgical history: Generally healthy; menstrual cramps occasionally. Last period two weeks ago.
- Medications: Vitamin D daily; occasional ibuprofen for cramps (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Social/occupational: Graphic designer; missed work (working from home). Non-smoker; occasional alcohol use.
- Review of systems: No rash; no blood in stool or urine reported; no other systemic symptoms noted.

Past Medical History:
- Chronic illnesses: none reported.
- Allergies: none reported.
- Medications: Vitamin D daily; ibuprofen occasionally (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Physical Examination:
- Vital signs: Not recorded.
- General: Not recorded.
- Abdominal: Periumbilical tenderness; pain prevents full palpation; cramping with intermittent urge to evacuate.
- Hydration/urine: Urine produced; last urination ~1 hour ago; no blood in stool or urine; no rash.
- Other: No additional signs documented.

Impression:
- Acute infectious gastroenteritis with dehydration risk.
- Top differentials (consistent with transcript):
  - Acute infectious gastroenteritis (viral preferred; possible bacterial etiologies considered).
  - Dehydration/electrolyte disturbances secondary to gastroenteritis.

- Conflict noted: none between transcript and differential.

Management Plan:
- Immediate actions and monitoring:
  - Urgent clinic appointment for hydration assessment and stool sample collection.
  - Continue oral rehydration salts with small, frequent sips to avoid vomiting; if unable to retain fluids, seek urgent care.
  - Light, easily digestible foods (e.g., toast, biscuits); avoid dairy, high-fiber fruits/vegetables, and milk until symptoms improve.
  - Monitor urine output; seek care if decreasing urine or signs of dehydration (dizziness, dry skin/mucous membranes, confusion).
- Investigations:
  - Stool sample to evaluate for bacterial infection and guide therapy; aim to process promptly at the clinic.
- Medications and reconciliations:
  - Oral rehydration solution continued; no new medications prescribed today.
  - Ibuprofen use previously reported; dose/route/frequency not documented; no changes to regimen documented.
- Follow-up:
  - Book urgent appointment via support line; if symptoms worsen, go to A&E promptly.

Patient Summary:
- The patient presents with about 3 days of acute gastroenteritis symptoms—very loose stools, fever, and vomiting with abdominal cramping. She is having trouble keeping fluids down but still urinates. An urgent clinic visit is arranged to assess hydration and obtain a stool sample; she will continue ORS and follow a light diet while awaiting test results.

Key Takeaways:
- Maintain oral rehydration with small, frequent sips; continue ORS even if vomiting.
- Seek urgent care if dehydration signs develop or if she cannot keep fluids down; await stool testing results to distinguish viral vs. bacterial etiologies.
- Eat light, bland foods and avoid dairy, fruits, vegetables, and milk until symptoms improve.

Next Steps:
- Attend urgent clinic appointment for stool sample collection and hydration assessment today.
- If feeling worse or unable to take fluids, seek A&E care.
- Continue ORS and monitor hydration status; follow-up based on test results and clinical course.
